approachQuestion.prompt:
Next cycling label

A read-only nondecreasing random-access array of integer labels forms a cycle. Given x, return the smallest label strictly greater than x, or the smallest array label if none is greater. Duplicates are allowed. 1<=n<=200000. Examples: [2,2,6,9], x=2 -> 6; x=9 -> 2; [4,4], x=4 -> 4. Prefer worst-case probes, then memory.
constraints: Use only the stated input ordering and access guarantees.

options.text: Find the first index with value >x by iterative upper-bound search. Return that label if the index is below n; otherwise return a[0].
options.feedback: Strict successor uses an upper bound, and a missing successor is a cycle boundary rather than an absent-result error.

options.text: Recursively search for the same strict upper bound using index bounds, then apply the same wrap rule.
options.feedback: This is correct, but recursion consumes avoidable stack memory.

options.text: Find the first value >=x and return it, wrapping only when that boundary is n.
options.feedback: For [2,2,6,9], x=2 this returns 2, violating strictness; the answer is 6.

Strictly greater requires upper_bound rather than lower_bound, especially when x itself occurs repeatedly. If the boundary is n, cycling returns the first label; it is not a failed lookup.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For target-method, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Analyze only the iterative strict upper-bound search and one final wrap check. Array access and comparisons are constant time; no copies or recursion. Input storage and returned result storage are excluded; all temporary buffers and call stacks are included.
constraints: Use worst-case bounds. Count all working memory including any stack; exclude supplied inputs and the scalar result.

feedback.reason: One strict upper-bound search and a final wrap check use scalar state.
details: Upper-bound comparisons halve n candidate positions, so search costs O(log(n+1)); selecting a[0] on wrap adds one access. Repeated equal values still permit half elimination because the predicate is strictly greater than x.
“O(log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Strict successor uses an upper bound, and a missing successor is a cycle boundary rather than an absent-result error.
“O(n*n + 1) time, O(n + 1) auxiliary space”: One strict upper-bound search halves the interval; wrapping adds one check, not pairwise work or a copied array.
“O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: A strict successor among n labels may require logarithmically many comparisons before the final wrap decision.
